paragraphs.text: Lesson 16, staying at a hotel.
Nolan and Beth are a married couple who are staying at a hotel on vacation.
Listen to their conversation and answer the questions.
We're really paying through the nose for this hotel.
Nolan, please don't start griping about the price.
We're on vacation.
Now's not the time to pinch pennies.
Yeah, but we're shelling out $2,000 for a week here.
We'll be broke by the end of the trip.
After a whole year of working like dogs, don't we deserve to treat ourselves to something nice?
Besides, there's the Gourmet restaurant and the meals are included with the price of our room.
Hm, Gourmet.
Usually means you pay top dollar for a tiny portion, arranged all artistically on the plate, of course.
Oh, you just don't know how to appreciate the finer things in life.
I can appreciate them, as long as I can have seconds.
I'm sure the meals are delicious and filling, Nolan.
Will you stop being so grumpy?
Just look at this lobby.
It's so elegant with all the antique furniture.
Probably fake.
Be that as it may, it's still gorgeous.
And you did brag about our room to your pals back in Chicago.
Well, yeah, but the daily rate is still highway robbery.
You're just sulking because you didn't get the discount you wanted.
I told you it wasn't valid here in Paris.
But it was at our hotel in London last year.
I can't believe this place refused to take my community club discount.
We do a lot of work for charity.
Is it too much to ask that we get 10% off travel expenses?
Well, then our next trip will be in the US.
How about to a log cabin in the middle of nowhere?
Then at least you'd get your precious discount.
Hey, no need to get snippy.
All I said was that $2,000 is a lot.
But now we've already paid.
I guess we might as well make the most of it.
Exactly.
I'm gonna go get a manicure at the beauty parlor.
Why don't you wait for me in the bar?
Have yourself a drink?
Maybe it'll help you loosen up.
Afterwards, we'll try the restaurant.
Jeez, are you planning on seeing Paris at all?
Or just spending the whole time in the hotel?
You're impossible.
Why do you always-
Hey, don't jump down my throat.
I was just messing with you.
It's too late to go out now anyway.
We'll just unwind tonight and then get an early start on our sightseeing tomorrow morning.
Let's learn the vocabulary from today's dialogue.
Nolan says, we're really paying through the nose for this hotel.
The expression paying through the nose means paying a lot of money,
often too much money for what you are getting.
Beth tells Nolan, please don't start griping about the price.
The word griping is another way to say complaining.
Beth says, we're on vacation.
Now's not the time to pinch pennies.
Pinch pennies means try to save every little bit of money.
The word penny refers to one cent in the United States.
Nolan replies, yeah, but we're shelling out 2,000 bucks for a week here.
The phrasal verb shelling out is another way to say spending,
especially spending a large amount of money.
And the word box is slang for dollars.
Nolan adds, we'll be broke by the end of our trip.
To be broke means to have no money available.
Beth reasons, after a whole year of working like dogs don't we deserve to treat ourselves to something nice?
The expression working like dogs means working very hard, often at a job that's difficult or unpleasant.
And treat ourselves means give ourselves something special or pleasant.
Besides, Beth says, there's a gourmet restaurant.
The word gourmet means fancy or very nice quality.
But Nolan says that gourmet usually means you pay top dollar for a tiny portion.
Top dollar is another way to say a high price.
And a portion is an amount of food.
But Nolan says he can appreciate gourmet food as long as he can have seconds.
Seconds means a second portion of food after you have eaten the first portion.
Beth replies, I'm sure the meals are delicious and filling.
If a food or a meal is filling, it means it is substantial.
It has enough substance or calories to satisfy your hunger.
Beth tells Nolan to stop being so grumpy.
If you are grumpy, it means you're in a bad mood.
Then she says, just look at this lobby.
It's so elegant with all the antique furniture.
The lobby is the reception or waiting area of the hotel.
And antique means very old.
Nolan suggests that the furniture is fake.
And Beth responds, be that as it may, it's still gorgeous.
The expression be that as it may means even if what you say is true.
And the word gorgeous means very beautiful.
Beth points out, you did brag about our room to your pals back in Chicago.
To brag about something means to speak arrogantly about something as though you are superior.
And the word pals is another way to say friends.
Nolan admits that he did do this, but he says the daily rate at the hotel is still highway robbery.
Highway robbery is an informal way to say charging a ridiculously high fee or price.
Beth says that Nolan is just sulking because he didn't get the discount he wanted.
The word sulking means to act angry and withdrawn, closing yourself off from other people because
of something bad or unfair that happened.
Children often sulk and it's considered a rather immature action.
Nolan says that his community club does a lot of work for charity.
And he says, is it too much to ask that we get 10% off travel expenses?
This expression, is it too much to ask, means this is not unreasonable.
In other words, it's reasonable to get 10% off.
And Beth gives a sarcastic reply, suggesting that their next trip be to a log cabin in the
middle of nowhere.
In the middle of nowhere means in a very isolated place, far from civilization.
Nolan replies, hey, no need to get snippy.
Snippy means saying things that can be sharp and hurtful.
And Nolan says, now that we've already paid the $2,000, I guess we should make the most of it.
Make the most of it means to get the most advantage or benefit out of this situation.
Especially if the situation is temporary or the situation is not so good.
Beth agrees with him and says, I'm going to go get a manicure at the beauty parlor.
A manicure means having one's fingernails cared for and painted.
Beth recommends that Nolan go to the bar and have a drink.
Maybe it'll help him loosen up.
Loosen up means to relax, be more friendly and less tense.
And then Nolan asks Beth a sarcastic question, to which she responds angrily.
Nolan then says, hey, don't jump down my throat.
To jump down someone's throat means to suddenly and strongly criticize, disagree with or get angry at someone.
Nolan says, I was just messing with you.
Messing with you means bothering or annoying you.
Finally, Nolan says, we'll just unwind tonight.
Unwind means to become relaxed after being stressed or tense.
Well, I hope Nolan and Beth can enjoy their stay at this hotel.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
